question: What is the largest organ system in the human body?
explanation: Great start! The integumentary system covers your entire body and includes your skin, hair, and nails. Think of it as your body's ultimate protective suit—and yes, it's our biggest organ system! [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which layer of the skin acts as the anchor, attaching the skin to muscles and bones underneath?
explanation: Spot on! The hypodermis (also called the subcutaneous layer) sits right at the bottom, holding your skin securely to the structures underneath like muscles and bones. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which layer of the epidermis is busy making new skin cells and producing melanin for color?
explanation: You got it! The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis where cell division happens constantly, and special cells called melanocytes make our skin pigment. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why does the outer layer of the skin (epidermis) have to rely on diffusion to get its nutrients?

options.A: It is made entirely of dead cells.
options.B: It repels blood vessels using keratin.
options.C: It is too thick for capillaries to enter.
options.D: It lacks a direct blood supply.

explanation: Exactly! The epidermis doesn't have its own blood vessels (it's avascular). Because of this, nutrients have to quietly seep up from the dermis living right below it. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which tiny structures in the upper dermis are responsible for giving you your unique fingerprints?
explanation: Well done! Dermal papillae are finger-like bumps that press up against the epidermis, creating those lovely ridges we know as fingerprints while helping supply nutrients. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h3)

question: What type of tissue gives the deeper part of the dermis (the reticular layer) its tough, stretchy strength?
explanation: You're crushing it! Dense irregular connective tissue handles pulls and stretches from all different directions, keeping our skin strong and resilient. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main type of tissue you will find in the hypodermis?
explanation: Correct! The hypodermis is packed with adipose (fat) tissue, which helps keep us warm, stores energy, and cushions us from bumps. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h4)

question: As a nurse, why is the subcutaneous layer (hypodermis) often chosen for giving certain injections?

options.A: It contains large blood vessels for steady drug absorption.
options.B: It prevents medications from entering the systemic circulation.
options.C: It lacks nerve endings, making injections completely painless.
options.D: It consists of hard bone that stabilizes the needle.

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! The hypodermis has a great blood supply, which allows injected medications to absorb smoothly and reliably into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h4)

question: What tiny muscle attached to hair follicles pulls hair upright to give us goosebumps?
explanation: You nailed it! The arrector pili is a tiny smooth muscle that contracts when we're cold or scared, pulling our hair follicles straight up. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h5)

question: Where does the continuous growth of a human nail actually start?
explanation: Brilliant! The nail matrix is the active growth zone hiding beneath the skin right at the base of the nail, constantly producing new cells. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which skin gland makes an oily substance called sebum to keep your hair and skin soft?
explanation: Correct! Sebaceous glands are our natural oil producers, keeping our skin waterproofed and conditioned. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main job of our everyday eccrine sweat glands?
explanation: You got it! Eccrine glands release water onto our skin, cooling us down as it evaporates when our body temperature rises. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which sensory receptors deep in the skin are great at detecting deep pressure and heavy vibrations?
explanation: Spot on! Pacinian corpuscles are shaped like tiny onions and sit deep in the skin to sense firm pressure and vibrations. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h7)

question: As a nursing student, what major clinical risk should you watch out for in patients who lose skin sensation due to nerve damage?

options.B: Rapid hair loss across the body

explanation: Crucial nursing insight! If patients can't feel pain or pressure, they won't notice cuts, burns, or pressure sores, which can easily turn into dangerous ulcers if we don't protect them. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h7)

question: What do the blood vessels in your skin do when your body temperature gets too high and you need to cool down?
explanation: You're right! They vasodilate (open wider) to bring more warm blood close to the surface, letting excess body heat escape into the air. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h8)

question: How does your skin play a vital role in keeping your bones strong with calcium?

options.A: By filtering calcium out through the sebaceous glands
options.B: By synthesizing vitamin D precursors using UV light
options.C: By storing dietary calcium directly in the epidermis

explanation: Fantastic! Sunlight hits the skin to jumpstart vitamin D production, which your gut needs to absorb calcium properly. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h8)
